title: Dissecting an instruction
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Castelino dissects how she gives classroom instructions, starting with the early-career version that triggered a flood of student questions and the overcorrected version that piled up so many directions that students could not hold them. She concludes that explicit instructions depend on several things beyond the wording itself. These are well-designed worked examples with faded support, front-loaded means of participation (FLMOP), routines that carry the logistics, and signposting of resources students can consult when stuck. The final instruction is short but not vague, because it leans on what students already know. The piece is a practical, evidence-informed account of making explicit instruction work in a science classroom.
points: Vague instructions and overlong instructions fail for opposite reasons, and both generate questions and lost time.
Students who have not seen worked examples for each question type struggle to work independently, so faded worked examples come first.
FLMOP, stating the location or means of participation before the task, makes students more likely to follow the whole instruction.
Routines such as fixed locations for equipment let a single cue phrase replace a string of steps.
Signposting conversion keys and notes teaches students where to look when stuck, including for homework and revision.
quotes: I am sure you can imagine that this did not actually stop the questions and instead added to the time it took to do anything in my lessons. It also meant students were so overwhelmed with all these instructions that they didn’t really have much chance to remember them all!

The first lesson I learnt was that if students hadn’t been shown exactly what to do when faced with different questions, they would struggle to complete them indepedently. Obviously, there are exceptions but I have found this to be true for the majority of the students I teach.

In the past, I would display an equation, show one or two examples that were already on a powerpoint and that would be it. And then, when asked to complete questions independently, I would spend several minutes providing support to students as I walked around the room. Too much lost time!
Students are more likely to listen to and follow the full instruction. Read this by Adam Boxer to find out exactly why this is such a powerful technique.

Students know that if they need any equipment (that I can provide), there is a particular place they can find them. For instance, glue sticks are in a tray at the front of the room. Mini-whiteboard pens are in a pot, one for each row.

For instance, when calculating magnification, students may need to convert units. Whilst this could (and should) be covered in the worked examples or pre-requisite knowledge check, it is not possible to cover all the different unit conversions. In these cases, it is important for students to know where to look so they can still work and, indeed, troubleshoot indepedently.

Doing it this way, I remind students that the worked examples are linked to the independent practice, so they know to look at them if stuck. I give them an idea of how many questions I expect them to complete in ten minutes. I provide the page number of the questions as the last bit of information so that students pay attention to the whole instruction.
